UAP LAB · “GoFast” Navy infrared video

The ocean-surface ATFLIR clip (recorded 2015, released by the Pentagon in April 2020) as cut into an ABC News report. Items marked measured were extracted from your file frame by frame; HUD means I read the on-screen number by eye from enlarged crops; modelled rests on stated assumptions. The file opens with 4 teaser frames showing the clip’s end state (53° L, 3.7 RNG) before cutting to the start; they are excluded from every chart.

Footage · thermal palette · sea-relative trail

0.0 s
ViewSpeed
Green ring = the pod’s lock point (it re-centres at ≈12 s when the square/tick acquisition symbols give way to the “|-|” bracket). Trail = where the locked point has been relative to the sea texture, using the measured sea scroll.

Lock point · 4× zoom raw pixels

Before ≈12 s the gate holds a faint smudge (below my 18-grey-level threshold). After, a compact speck sits in the bracket: bright in black-hot, dark in the white-hot window (≈21.4–26.3 s).

Locked point vs the sea measured

Cumulative sea scroll (px, y down) from phase correlation of the lower sea area, 9-frame median. The pod holds the point at screen centre, so the sea streams past instead.

Sea-surface scroll speed measured

px/s in the image. Near zero while the pod is still acquiring, then ≈400–470 px/s at the lock hand-off, decaying to ≈60–80 px/s by the end. Phase-correlation confidence is modest (0.1–0.3) because the sea texture is low-contrast and compressed: read the shape, not individual values.

HUD readings

Green: azimuth, “NN° L” (35→58). Orange: elevation magnitude (22→35). Blue: range ×10 (RNG appears at ≈12.5 s, 4.4→3.3; unit assumed nmi). Read every second, ±1 unit.

Brightness: sea level and speck contrast

0–255 display grey, not temperature. Speck contrast (orange) flips from ≈+120 to ≈−57 exactly when the sea level (white) jumps ≈19 → ≈55 grey levels at ≈21.4 s and back at ≈26.3 s: one contrast changing sign with polarity, not an overlay. Short dips near 10 s and 19 s are gain changes.

Roll and texture direction measured

Orange: tilt of the aircraft-symbol wing line (+ = right side down), 0° → ≈14° within ≈1.5 s near 17 s: the jet rolls into a bank. Green: sea-streak direction minus 180°; it shifts ≈ −12° around 12 s, at the lock hand-off, not at the bank.

Closing-speed lab modelled

One infrared camera gives angles, not distance. But the HUD also prints range and a second number (210→150) that tracks the range rate. If the jet flies straight at Mach 0.61 (≈375 kt TAS at 25,000 ft, ISA) and the object were stationary, the closing speed would be V·cos(az)·cos(el). Compare that with what the HUD says; any gap is motion of the object along the line of sight. Sideways motion cannot be seen by this test.
Moment
Pod-angle / pitch error
Assumed field of view
Green: closing speed expected for a stationary target. Orange: HUD readout. Blue: range difference over ±3 s (RNG is quantised to 0.1 nmi). The gap is ≈25–30 kt for most of the clip and ≈15 kt at the end: the HUD numbers are consistent with an object moving at most a few tens of knots along the line of sight. A 5° pitch error moves the prediction by ≈10 kt, so this is a consistency check, not a speed measurement. Altitude puzzle: from 25,000 ft a sea-level target cannot be closer than 4.11 nmi slant range, yet RNG falls to 3.3, so either RNG is not slant nmi to the sea, or the object is well above the surface (≈13,500 ft if elevation is measured from the horizon).

Competing explanations vs. what was measured

HypothesisFitsStrains
Slow or stationary object, speed illusion from parallax (argued by several independent analysts)Speck stays locked at screen centre at a constant tiny size; the sea scrolls ≈300 px/s then slows, as expected for a camera sweeping over a surface; HUD closing speed matches a stationary target to within ≈15–30 kt.Needs range and altitude that are not in the clip; the 3.3 nmi vs 25,000 ft puzzle means the object cannot be at sea level if RNG is slant nmi.
Genuinely fast anomalous object (the framing in the original pilot-and-press coverage)Fast apparent motion over the water is real in the image; no wings, exhaust or structure visible.The apparent motion is mostly the sea’s scroll caused by the pod’s own geometry; no independent track published; absent features are expected at a few pixels.
Sensor / processing artefactPolarity switch, gate hand-off at ≈12 s, roll and gain changes visibly alter the picture.Does not by itself explain a persistent compact speck that follows the polarity inversion.
Status: the footage was released by the Department of Defense as unexplained, and no public source here establishes what the object is. Treat all three hypotheses as open.

Method and limits

1,033 frames at 29.97 fps, 1280×720; the sensor picture (640×640 at x=317, y=42) was analysed after dropping the 4 teaser frames (1,029 frames, 34.3 s). Sea scroll: windowed phase correlation of a high-passed 400×200 patch below the lock point, frames with confidence <0.04 zeroed (≈18%), 9-frame median. Speck: 7×7 patch at the lock point versus the median of the surrounding 120×120 area, count of pixels differing by >18 grey levels; it fills the window (≈40 of 49 px), so the true size is only bounded from above and may include the tracker’s centre mark. Texture direction: structure tensor of the sea patch. Roll: line fit to the brightest pixels of the aircraft-symbol wing line. HUD: azimuth, elevation, range, second readout, Mach and altitude read by eye each second (±1 unit); the second readout’s unit and meaning are inferred from its match to the range rate. Pixel values are display grey, not temperature, and I do not know the pod’s true field of view (slider). No claim here identifies the object.
